name: Yield curve
definition: A curve that plots the yields of bonds of the same credit quality (typically government securities) against their times to maturity at a given point in time. The U.S. Treasury's official version is a par yield curve relating the par yield on a Treasury security to its time to maturity, derived daily from market price quotations.
intuition: It is a snapshot of what it costs to borrow money for different lengths of time, showing how the market prices time, risk, and expectations about future rates.
mechanics: Market prices of on-the-run securities are converted to yields, and a curve-fitting method (Treasury uses bootstrapping of forward rates plus monotone convex interpolation) produces a continuous curve from which constant-maturity yields are read.
failure_modes: Curve shapes mix expected future rates, term premia, and supply/demand effects, so the curve alone cannot identify which driver dominates. Fitted curves are also model-dependent: different fitting methods produce slightly different yields at the same maturities.
misconceptions: A common mistake is treating the yield curve as a forecast of future rates; Treasury itself states that the curve indicates what rates were and are, not what they will be.
example: On a day when the 2-year Treasury yields 4.0% and the 10-year yields 4.3%, the 2s10s segment of the curve is upward sloping by 30 basis points.

name: Normal yield curve
definition: A yield curve configuration in which longer-maturity yields are higher than shorter-maturity yields, giving the curve an upward slope. It is the historically most common configuration, reflecting term premia and typical expectations that rates will not fall sharply.
intuition: Lenders usually demand more compensation for tying up money longer, so longer loans carry higher rates — that is the 'normal' state of the curve.
mechanics: The slope is measured as a spread between constant-maturity yields, e.g. the 10-year minus the 2-year Treasury yield; a positive value corresponds to a normal (upward-sloping) curve.
formula: Slope ≈ y(long maturity) − y(short maturity) > 0, e.g. 10-year CMT minus 2-year CMT.
failure_modes: An upward slope does not prove rates will rise; the slope conflates term premium, rate expectations, and issuance/demand effects, so reading it as a pure forecast is unreliable.
misconceptions: It is wrong to assume 'normal' means guaranteed or stable; curves can steepen or flatten quickly, and a normal curve is simply the modal historical shape, not a law.
example: If 3-month bills yield 3.5%, the 2-year note yields 4.0%, and the 10-year yields 4.5%, the curve is normal (upward sloping).

name: Inverted yield curve
definition: A yield curve configuration in which shorter-maturity yields exceed longer-maturity yields, giving the curve a downward slope. The U.S. Treasury notes that short-term rates can exceed longer-term rates when market expectations about future rates and monetary policy shift; inversions have historically preceded U.S. recessions, though the relationship is a statistical regularity, not a causal law.
intuition: Investors accept lower yields on long bonds because they expect rates to fall in the future — often because they expect the central bank to cut rates in a slowdown.
mechanics: Measured as a negative term spread, e.g. the 10-year Treasury constant maturity yield minus the 2-year (FRED series T10Y2Y) falling below zero. Inversions often arise when policy tightening pushes short rates up while long yields stay anchored by weak growth expectations.
formula: Inversion when y(short) − y(long) > 0, e.g. 2-year CMT − 10-year CMT > 0.
failure_modes: Inversions have produced false or very early recession signals, and post-2008 term premium compression (e.g. from quantitative easing) can invert curves without implying a downturn; timing between inversion and recession varies widely.
misconceptions: Inversion does not cause recessions, nor does it guarantee one; it is an indicator of market expectations and term premia, not a mechanical trigger.
example: In 2022–2023 the 2-year Treasury yield rose above the 10-year yield, leaving the 2s10s spread negative for an extended period.

name: Flat yield curve
definition: A yield curve configuration in which yields are approximately equal across maturities, so the term spread is near zero. It typically appears as a transitional state between an upward-sloping (normal) curve and an inverted curve, or vice versa.
intuition: The market is charging roughly the same rate to borrow for one year as for ten years — a sign that expectations about the future are unusually uncertain or in transition.
mechanics: Identified when the spread between long- and short-maturity constant-maturity yields (e.g. 10-year minus 2-year Treasury) is close to zero; flattening occurs when short rates rise toward long rates (bear flattener) or long rates fall toward short rates (bull flattener).
formula: Flat when |y(long) − y(short)| ≈ 0.
failure_modes: A flat curve carries little standalone signal: it can precede steepening or inversion, and 'flatness' has no precise threshold, so classification is judgment-dependent.
misconceptions: A flat curve is not a neutral or 'no information' state in a predictive sense, and it is not a distinct market regime with proven consequences — it is simply a descriptive shape.
example: If the 2-year Treasury yields 4.20% and the 10-year yields 4.25%, the 2s10s segment is essentially flat at 5 basis points.

name: Spot rate curve
definition: The curve of yields on zero-coupon instruments across maturities — the set of rates at which a single future cash flow is discounted to today. It is built by bootstrapping coupon-bearing bond prices so that each instrument is repriced without error, and it is the curve used for present-value calculations.
intuition: Instead of one blended yield per bond, the spot curve gives a separate 'pure' interest rate for every single future date, like a price tag for money delivered at each point in time.
mechanics: Starting from the shortest maturity, each bond's price is decomposed into its cash flows; the discount rate that prices each successive maturity's cash flow exactly (given already-solved shorter rates) is the spot rate for that maturity. The U.S. Treasury bootstraps instantaneous forward rates from on-the-run prices, which equivalently determines the spot curve; Treasury does not publish a daily zero-coupon curve itself.
formula: P = sum over t of CF_t / (1 + z_t)^t, where z_t is the t-year spot (zero-coupon) rate, CF_t the cash flow at time t, and P the bond's price.
failure_modes: The bootstrapped curve depends on the fitting/interpolation method and the input securities chosen, so different constructions give different spot rates, especially between quoted maturities and at the long end.
misconceptions: Spot rates are not directly observable in coupon-bond markets and are not the same as par yields; the par yield curve and the spot curve differ whenever the curve is not flat.
example: If the 2-year spot rate is 4.2%, a single $100 payment due in exactly 2 years is worth 100 / (1.042)^2 ≈ $92.10 today.

name: Forward rate curve
definition: The curve of interest rates implied today for borrowing or lending over future periods, derived from the spot (zero-coupon) curve so that investing to a long horizon equals rolling over at the shorter rate plus the forward rate. The U.S. Treasury's curve construction bootstraps instantaneous forward rates at input maturities as an intermediate step.
intuition: If you know the 1-year rate and the 2-year rate, the market is implicitly quoting a rate for year two alone — the forward curve is the set of all such implied future-period rates.
mechanics: Forward rates are extracted from spot rates by no-arbitrage: chaining the short spot rate with the forward rate over the remaining period must reproduce the long spot rate. Treasury derives instantaneous forward rates so that input securities are sequentially priced without error.
formula: (1 + z_T)^T = (1 + z_t)^t × (1 + f(t,T))^(T−t), so f(t,T) = [ (1 + z_T)^T / (1 + z_t)^t ]^(1/(T−t)) − 1, where z_t, z_T are spot rates and f(t,T) is the forward rate from t to T.
failure_modes: Forward rates embed term and risk premia, so they are biased predictors of realized future rates; empirically the expectations hypothesis performs poorly, especially at longer horizons.
misconceptions: An implied forward rate is not a market forecast agreed by participants; it is an arithmetic consequence of today's spot curve plus premia, not a prediction.
example: If the 1-year spot rate is 4.0% and the 2-year spot rate is 4.5%, the implied 1-year forward rate one year ahead is (1.045^2 / 1.04) − 1 ≈ 5.0%.

citations.source: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Treasury Yield Curve Methodology

name: Discount factor
definition: The present value of one unit of currency received at a specified future date, equivalently the price today of a risk-free zero-coupon payment of 1 at that date. The full set of discount factors across dates is the discount function, which is derived from the spot rate curve.
intuition: A discount factor answers: how much is a dollar delivered on a given future date worth right now?
mechanics: Each cash flow of an instrument is multiplied by the discount factor for its payment date and summed to get the instrument's present value. Discount factors are obtained from spot rates (or, equivalently, from the bootstrapped forward-rate curve used in curve construction such as Treasury's).
formula: DF(t) = 1 / (1 + z_t)^t with annual compounding (DF(t) = e^(−z_t × t) under continuous compounding), where z_t is the t-year spot rate; PV = Σ CF_t × DF(t).
failure_modes: Because discount factors inherit the chosen curve-fitting method and day-count/compounding conventions, they can differ across vendors even for the same date; using a single yield for all maturities instead of term-specific factors misprices non-standard cash flows.
misconceptions: A discount factor is not a 'discount' in the retail sense and is not the same as a coupon rate; it is a present-value weight between 0 and 1 for a specific date.
example: With a 2-year spot rate of 4%, the 2-year discount factor is 1 / 1.04^2 ≈ 0.9246, so $1,000 due in 2 years is worth about $924.60 today.

citations.source: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Treasury Yield Curve Methodology

name: Zero-coupon rate
definition: The yield earned on an investment that makes a single payment at maturity with no intermediate coupons, for a specific maturity. It is the building block of the spot (zero-coupon) curve used to discount individual future cash flows.
intuition: It is the pure interest rate for money delivered at one exact future date, with nothing paid in between — like the rate on a Treasury bill or a STRIP.
mechanics: For a zero-coupon instrument the rate follows directly from price and face value; for coupon-bearing markets the zero-coupon rates are bootstrapped from bond prices so all input securities price without error. The U.S. Treasury notes its published par yield curve is a semiannual bond-equivalent curve and that it does not publish daily zero-coupon curve rates.
formula: z_t = (F / P)^(1/t) − 1, where P is the price today, F the single payment at maturity, and t the time in years.
failure_modes: Zero-coupon rates are model-derived rather than directly quoted for most maturities, so they inherit bootstrapping and interpolation assumptions; liquidity differences between coupon bonds and STRIPS can also create small inconsistencies.
misconceptions: The zero-coupon rate for maturity t is not the yield of the t-year coupon bond; confusing par yields with spot rates produces systematic valuation errors when the curve is sloped.
example: A 2-year zero-coupon bond priced at 92.10 per 100 face implies a 2-year zero rate of (100/92.10)^(1/2) − 1 ≈ 4.2%.

name: Par yield
definition: The coupon rate at which a hypothetical bond of a given maturity would price exactly at par (100% of face value), given the current discount function. The U.S. Treasury's official daily yield curve is a par yield curve, and its constant-maturity (CMT) rates are par yields read from that curve.
intuition: It is the coupon a brand-new bond of a given maturity would have to pay today for investors to accept it at full face value.
mechanics: Treasury converts indicative bid-side price quotations on the most recently auctioned securities to yields, bootstraps forward rates, and applies monotone convex interpolation to construct a curve of true par rates; CMT yields are then read at fixed maturities and quoted as semiannual bond-equivalent yields.
formula: Par coupon c solves 100 = Σ_t (c/2) × DF(t) + 100 × DF(T), where DF(t) are discount factors and T is maturity (semiannual coupons).
failure_modes: CMT par yields are read from a fitted curve and may not match the actual yield of any specific traded security; the curve also depends on the fitting methodology, which Treasury has changed over time.
misconceptions: A par yield is not the same as the spot rate for that maturity, and a CMT rate is not the yield on an actual outstanding bond of exactly that maturity.
example: If the fitted 10-year par yield is 4.30%, a new theoretical 10-year bond with a 4.30% coupon would be worth exactly 100.

name: Yield spread
definition: The difference between two yields, typically expressed in basis points. Depending on context it may compare maturities on the same curve (term spread, e.g. 10-year minus 2-year Treasury), or securities of different credit quality at the same maturity (credit spread).
intuition: It is the extra (or lesser) yield one instrument offers relative to another, summarizing how the market prices the difference in time, risk, or liquidity between them.
mechanics: Computed as a simple subtraction of yields at matched or specified maturities; e.g. FRED's T10Y2Y is the 10-year Treasury constant maturity yield minus the 2-year, and term or credit spreads widen or narrow as relative yields move.
formula: s = y_A − y_B, quoted in basis points (1 bp = 0.01 percentage point).
failure_modes: A raw yield spread ignores differences in maturity, coupon, embedded options, and compounding conventions, so comparing spreads across unlike instruments can mislead; spreads also mix risk, liquidity, and tax effects.
misconceptions: A wider spread does not automatically mean a bond is 'cheap'; it may simply reflect genuinely higher expected losses or worse liquidity.
example: If a 10-year corporate bond yields 5.6% and the 10-year Treasury yields 4.3%, the yield spread is 130 basis points.

name: Credit spread
definition: The difference between the yield on the debt securities of a particular corporate or sovereign borrower (or a rating class of borrowers) and the yield on similar-maturity Treasury securities. It compensates investors for bearing default and credit-migration risk, plus a liquidity component.
intuition: It is the extra interest a risky borrower must pay over the government to persuade investors to lend to it.
mechanics: Measured as corporate (or other non-Treasury) yield minus the matched-maturity Treasury yield, or at index level as an option-adjusted spread over the Treasury spot curve, e.g. the ICE BofA US Corporate Index OAS published on FRED.
formula: Credit spread = y(corporate bond) − y(matched-maturity Treasury), in basis points.
failure_modes: Spreads conflate expected default losses, risk premia, and illiquidity, so they overstate pure default compensation; in crises, liquidity-driven widening can look like surging default risk. Maturity or option mismatches also distort simple yield differences.
misconceptions: The credit spread is not a direct estimate of default probability, and a high spread does not by itself imply a mispricing or an attractive trade.
example: If BBB-rated 10-year corporate bonds yield 5.5% while the 10-year Treasury yields 4.3%, the credit spread is 120 basis points.

name: Option-adjusted spread
definition: The constant spread added to a benchmark spot curve that makes the model value of a security's cash flows — adjusted for the value of embedded options such as calls or prepayment rights — equal to its market price. It is the standard spread measure for callable bonds and mortgage-backed securities.
intuition: It is the yield premium a bond pays over Treasuries after stripping out the value of any options hidden in the bond, leaving a cleaner measure of credit and liquidity compensation.
mechanics: An interest-rate model generates many rate paths; cash flows on each path reflect option exercise (e.g. calls or prepayments). The spread over the benchmark curve that equates the average present value across paths to the market price is the OAS. ICE BofA computes index OAS as the market-cap-weighted average of constituent bond OAS versus a spot Treasury curve.
formula: Price = (1/N) Σ_paths Σ_t CF_t(path) × DF_t(path; benchmark + OAS); OAS is solved numerically.
failure_modes: OAS is model-dependent: results vary with the volatility assumptions and interest-rate/prepayment model used, so OAS values from different models are not strictly comparable. It is also an average over scenarios, not a guaranteed earned spread.
misconceptions: OAS is not the spread an investor will actually realize; realized excess return depends on path, default, and prepayment outcomes, not just the option adjustment.
example: The ICE BofA US Corporate Index OAS (FRED series BAMLC0A0CM) stood around 0.8–1.0% in calm periods and spiked above 4% in March 2020, reflecting the market-wide corporate spread adjustment over the Treasury spot curve.

citations.source: FRED, ICE BofA US Corporate Index Option-Adjusted Spread [BAMLC0A0CM] (source: ICE Data Indices)

name: Z-spread
definition: The constant spread that, when added to each point of the Treasury (or benchmark) spot rate curve, makes the present value of a bond's cash flows equal to its market price. Unlike a nominal spread measured at a single maturity, it accounts for the entire term structure; unlike OAS, it does not adjust for embedded options.
intuition: It is the single number of extra yield the bond must offer at every point along the curve for its promised cash flows to be worth today's price.
mechanics: Each cash flow is discounted at the benchmark spot rate for its maturity plus the spread Z; Z is solved numerically so the discounted cash flows sum to the full (dirty) price. For option-free bonds the Z-spread and OAS coincide; for bonds with embedded options the Z-spread includes compensation for option risk.
formula: P = Σ_t CF_t / (1 + (z_t + Z)/2)^(2t), where P is the full price, CF_t the cash flow at time t, z_t the spot rate at t, and Z the Z-spread (semiannual convention).
failure_modes: For callable or prepayable bonds the Z-spread misattributes option value to credit/liquidity, overstating the option-free spread; it also assumes cash flows are certain, so it is misleading for credit-risky securities near distress.
misconceptions: The 'zero-volatility' name does not mean the bond is riskless; it means the spread is constant and no interest-rate volatility model (option adjustment) is applied.
example: A 3-year bond priced at 104.90 with cash flows of 5, 5, and 105 against spot rates of 2.5%, 2.7%, and 3.0% has a Z-spread of about 0.29% (29 bp).

name: Asset swap spread
definition: The spread over the floating benchmark in an asset swap — a package in which an investor buys a fixed-rate bond and simultaneously enters an interest rate swap, paying the bond's fixed coupons and receiving a floating rate plus a spread. It expresses the bond's yield relative to the swap curve rather than to government bonds.
intuition: It measures how much extra return a bond offers once its interest-rate exposure has been swapped away, isolating the credit and liquidity premium versus the derivatives market's benchmark.
mechanics: In a par asset swap, the investor pays the bond's fixed coupon into the swap and receives floating (e.g. SOFR) plus or minus a fixed spread; the package is priced at par, and the spread solves for the floating-leg margin. The asset swap spread is thus the difference between the bond's economics and the matched-maturity swap rate, expressed in basis points.
formula: ASW spread ≈ bond's spread over the swap curve such that (bond price + swap value) = par at inception; roughly ASW ≈ (bond yield − swap rate) adjusted for any premium/discount to par amortized over the swap.
failure_modes: The spread depends on the swap benchmark and the assumed funding of the position; benchmark transitions (LIBOR to SOFR) changed its level and comparability. Unlike a CDS, an asset swap does not terminate on default, so it embeds recovery-risk differences.
misconceptions: A high asset swap spread does not mean the position is protected against default — the investor keeps the bond's credit risk, since the swap typically continues even if the issuer defaults.
example: An investor buys a bond yielding 6% when the matched swap rate is 5%; after accounting for the price premium, the asset swap spread might be quoted as SOFR + 50 bp.

name: Swap spread
definition: The difference between the fixed rate on a plain-vanilla interest rate swap of a given maturity and the yield on a government bond of the same maturity. It reflects the relative pricing of the derivatives and government bond markets, including intermediation and funding costs.
intuition: It compares the cost of exchanging fixed-for-floating payments in the swap market with the government's borrowing cost — a gauge of how dealers price balance-sheet usage and of relative supply and demand in the two markets.
mechanics: Swap rate minus same-maturity government bond yield, in basis points. Arbitrage links the two markets (hold the bond funded via repo, pay fixed on the swap), but dealer balance-sheet costs, repo funding rates, bond supply, and demand to receive fixed can push spreads away from zero; long-maturity USD spreads have been persistently negative in recent years, and the shift from LIBOR to risk-free rates such as SOFR mechanically lowered swap spreads.
formula: Swap spread = swap rate(maturity T) − government bond yield(maturity T), in basis points.
failure_modes: Spreads are not a pure credit measure: they move with repo funding costs, dealer constraints, Treasury supply, and benchmark conventions, so treating them as a simple risk gauge misleads. Negative spreads are not exploitable arbitrage profits — they compensate intermediaries for real balance-sheet costs.
misconceptions: A negative swap spread is not a 'free lunch' arbitrage left on the table; capturing it requires repo-funded bond holdings whose financing and balance-sheet costs consume the apparent profit.
example: If the 10-year SOFR swap rate is 3.60% and the 10-year Treasury yields 4.05%, the 10-year swap spread is −45 basis points.

citations.source: BIS Quarterly Review, December 2024 — 'Negative interest rate swap spreads signal pressure in government debt absorption'

name: DV01
aliases: dollar value of a basis point
definition: The change in a bond's (or portfolio's) value, in currency units, for a one-basis-point (0.01%) change in yield. In the U.S. it is also called the dollar value of an 01; it is essentially the price value of a basis point (PVBP), often written PV01.
intuition: It answers the trader's core question: how many dollars do I make or lose if yields move by one basis point?
mechanics: Computed either analytically as modified duration times full price times 0.0001, or numerically by repricing the position with yields shifted up and down one basis point and halving the difference. Because it is additive across positions, it is the standard unit for sizing and hedging interest-rate risk.
formula: DV01 = ModDur × P × 0.0001, where ModDur is modified duration and P the full price; equivalently DV01 = (PV(−1bp) − PV(+1bp)) / 2.
failure_modes: DV01 is a linear (first-order) sensitivity: for large yield moves it ignores convexity, so realized P&L deviates from the DV01 estimate. For option-embedded bonds it shifts with the level of rates.
misconceptions: DV01 is not a percentage and not a probability; and a DV01-hedged book is only hedged against small parallel yield moves, not against curve reshaping or volatility changes.
example: A bond with modified duration 8.5 and full price 101 has DV01 ≈ 8.5 × 101 × 0.0001 ≈ $0.0859 per $100 face — about $859 per $1 million face per basis point.

citations.source: AnalystPrep, CFA Level 1 Fixed Income — Modified Duration, Money Duration, and Price Value of a Basis Point (PVBP)

name: PV01
aliases: present value of a basis point
price value of a basis point
definition: The change in the present value (full price) of a bond or swap for a one-basis-point change in yield. It is the same quantity as PVBP and the U.S. market term DV01; in swap markets PV01 is the standard sensitivity measure per basis point of the swap rate.
intuition: It is the cash value gained or lost when the relevant rate ticks up or down by a single basis point.
mechanics: Estimated numerically by repricing with yields one basis point lower and one basis point higher and taking half the difference, which works even when cash flows are uncertain (e.g. callable bonds); analytically it equals modified duration times price times 0.0001.
failure_modes: Like all first-order sensitivities it ignores convexity and is valid only locally; PV01 quoted on swaps depends on curve-construction and discounting conventions, so cross-vendor values can differ slightly.
misconceptions: PV01 and DV01 are sometimes claimed to be fundamentally different measures; in practice both denote the present-value change per basis point, with naming differences by market segment rather than by concept.
example: If a swap's present value rises by $4,600 when its rate falls 1 bp and falls by $4,400 when the rate rises 1 bp, its PV01 ≈ (4,600 + 4,400)/2 = $4,500 per bp on the position.

name: Key rate duration
definition: A measure of a bond's or portfolio's price sensitivity to a change in yield at one specific maturity point on the curve, holding other points fixed. The set of key rate durations across maturities decomposes total interest-rate sensitivity, and they sum (approximately) to the effective duration.
intuition: Instead of asking 'what if all rates move?', it asks 'what if only the 5-year rate moves?' — locating where along the curve a portfolio's risk actually sits.
mechanics: The yield at a chosen key maturity (e.g. 2, 5, 10, 30 years) is shifted by a small amount (with the shift tapered to neighboring points), the security is repriced both ways, and duration is computed from the price changes; repeating across 11 standard maturities gives a sensitivity profile used for non-parallel curve hedging.
formula: KRD_i = (P(−) − P(+)) / (2 × Δy × P_0), where P(−), P(+) are prices after a 1% down/up shift of the key rate at maturity i, and P_0 the original price.
failure_modes: Real yield curves rarely move one point at a time, so isolated key rate shifts are artificial; results also depend on how the shift is tapered to adjacent maturities, making values convention-dependent.
misconceptions: A high total duration does not reveal curve exposure: two portfolios with the same effective duration can have very different key rate profiles and behave oppositely when the curve twists.
example: A portfolio with a 10-year key rate duration of 4.0 loses roughly 4% of value if the 10-year rate alone rises 100 bp, regardless of what other maturities do.

citations.source: Investopedia, Key Rate Duration

name: Effective duration
definition: A bond's price sensitivity to a parallel shift in the benchmark yield curve, computed numerically by repricing the bond at higher and lower yields while allowing cash flows to change (e.g. via call or prepayment options). It is the appropriate duration measure for bonds with embedded options, where cash flows are not fixed.
intuition: It measures how much a bond's price actually moves when rates move, recognizing that for callable or mortgage bonds the payments themselves change when rates change.
mechanics: The bond is valued under a small downward and upward parallel shift of the curve (using a model that adjusts cash flows for embedded options), and duration is approximated from the three prices; it equals the percentage price change for a 1% parallel rate move.
formula: EffDur = (P(−) − P(+)) / (2 × Δy × P_0), where P(−), P(+) are prices after a parallel curve shift down/up of Δy, and P_0 the current price.
failure_modes: It assumes parallel curve shifts, so it misses reshaping risk; it is also model-dependent for option-embedded bonds, since the prepayment or option model determines the shifted prices.
misconceptions: Duration is not the bond's maturity and not a fixed property of the security — effective duration changes as rates, volatility, and time move, especially for callable bonds.
example: If a callable bond priced at 100 would be worth 103.5 at rates 50 bp lower and 96.8 at rates 50 bp higher, its effective duration is (103.5 − 96.8)/(2 × 0.005 × 100) = 6.7.

name: Macaulay duration
definition: The weighted-average time until a bond's cash flows are received, with each cash flow weighted by its share of the bond's present value. Expressed in years, it equals maturity for a zero-coupon bond and is always shorter than maturity for a coupon bond; it is the foundation from which modified and effective duration are derived.
intuition: It is the 'center of gravity' of a bond's payments — the single point in time at which the average dollar of the bond's value arrives.
mechanics: Each cash flow's present value is divided by the bond's full price to get a weight; the weights are multiplied by the time to receipt and summed. Dividing Macaulay duration by (1 + yield per period) gives modified duration, the direct price-sensitivity measure.
formula: MacDur = Σ_t [ t × PV(CF_t) ] / P, where PV(CF_t) is the present value of the cash flow at time t and P the full price; ModDur = MacDur / (1 + r), with r the yield per period.
failure_modes: As a time measure it applies cleanly only to fixed cash flows; for callable or floating-rate instruments the cash-flow weights are not fixed, so Macaulay duration is undefined or misleading without an options model.
misconceptions: Duration in years is often mistaken for the bond's remaining life; a 10-year coupon bond's Macaulay duration is well below 10 years, and duration (not maturity) is what governs rate sensitivity.
example: A 4-year, 4% semiannual-pay bond at a 6% yield has an annualized Macaulay duration of about 3.72 years — less than its 4-year maturity because coupons arrive earlier.

citations.source: AnalystPrep, CFA Level 1 Fixed Income — Modified Duration, Money Duration, and Price Value of a Basis Point (PVBP)

name: Negative convexity
definition: A property of a bond whose price-yield relationship is concave: prices rise less when yields fall and fall more when yields rise than duration alone predicts. It is typical of callable bonds and mortgage-backed securities, whose cash flows shorten when rates decline (calls/prepayments) and lengthen when rates rise.
intuition: The bond works against you both ways: it stops appreciating just when rates fall (because it gets called or prepaid) and keeps falling when rates rise.
mechanics: Convexity is the second derivative of price with respect to yield, approximated as (P(−) + P(+) − 2P_0) / (P_0 × Δy²); when this quantity is negative, duration rises as yields rise (extension risk) and falls as yields fall (contraction risk), making duration-only hedges systematically wrong in the adverse direction.
formula: Convexity ≈ (P(−) + P(+) − 2 × P_0) / (P_0 × Δy²); negative when P(−) + P(+) < 2 × P_0.
failure_modes: Duration-based estimates fail precisely when they are most needed (large rate moves) for negatively convex securities; hedging MBS or callable books with duration alone creates pro-cyclical hedging flows that can amplify rate swings.
misconceptions: Negative convexity does not mean the bond must lose money; it means the price response is asymmetric, and investors are compensated for bearing it through higher yield (option-adjusted spread).
example: A callable bond priced at 100 might gain only 3 points if yields fall 100 bp (its price is capped near the call price) but lose 6 points if yields rise 100 bp.

citations.source: Investopedia, Negative Convexity

name: Positive convexity
definition: A property of a bond whose price-yield relationship is convex: prices rise more when yields fall and fall less when yields rise than duration alone predicts. All standard non-callable fixed-rate bonds exhibit positive convexity; the effect grows with longer maturity and lower coupons.
intuition: The bond's price accelerates in your favor: you gain a bit extra when rates fall and lose a bit less when rates rise, compared with the straight-line duration estimate.
mechanics: Convexity is the curvature (second derivative) of the price-yield function; with positive convexity, duration falls as yields rise and rises as yields fall. The effect is most pronounced in long-duration, low-coupon bonds, and the price impact is captured by adding a convexity adjustment to the duration estimate.
formula: Convexity ≈ (P(−) + P(+) − 2 × P_0) / (P_0 × Δy²) > 0; price change ≈ −ModDur × Δy × P_0 + ½ × Convexity × (Δy)² × P_0.
failure_modes: Convexity benefits are already priced in (higher-convexity bonds trade at lower yields), so it is not a free advantage; for small rate moves the convexity term is negligible and adds little to the duration estimate.
misconceptions: Positive convexity is not a guarantee of outperformance and does not mean prices cannot fall; it only describes the curvature of the price-yield relationship.
example: A 30-year zero-coupon bond has very high positive convexity: a 100 bp yield decline lifts its price by more than duration suggests, while a 100 bp rise costs it less.

citations.source: Fidelity, Duration: Understanding the Relationship Between Bond Prices and Interest Rates

name: Basis point
definition: A unit of measure for interest rates and yields equal to one one-hundredth of a percentage point (0.01%). It is the standard unit for quoting yield changes, spreads, and rate moves.
intuition: It is the 'cent' of interest rates: saying 'up 25 basis points' unambiguously means up 0.25 percentage points.
mechanics: Yields, spreads, and rate changes are multiplied by 100 to convert percentage points to basis points; e.g. the Federal Reserve describes changes in the federal funds target in basis points, and DV01 measures value change per one basis point.
formula: 1 bp = 0.01% = 0.0001 in decimal; value in bp = value in percent × 100.
failure_modes: Confusion between basis points and percent (or between relative percent change and percentage-point change) causes order-of-magnitude errors in P&L and risk calculations.
misconceptions: A '1% rise in rates' is ambiguous; professional usage distinguishes a 100 bp (one percentage point) rise from a 1 percent relative increase, which are very different.
example: If the 10-year Treasury yield moves from 4.25% to 4.50%, it has risen 25 basis points.

name: Policy rate
definition: The short-term interest rate that a central bank sets (or targets) to implement monetary policy. In the United States it is the Federal Open Market Committee's target range for the federal funds rate, which the New York Fed's trading desk defends through open market operations and administered rates.
intuition: It is the central bank's main dial: raising it tightens financial conditions to cool the economy, lowering it loosens conditions to stimulate activity.
mechanics: The FOMC announces a target range for the federal funds rate; the Desk conducts repo, reverse repo, and other operations, and sets administered rates (interest on reserve balances, ON RRP offering rate, standing repo rate) to keep the effective market rate within the range.
failure_modes: The policy rate directly anchors only very short-term rates; long-term yields are driven by expectations and term premia, so policy moves can fail to transmit (e.g. the 2000s 'conundrum' when long yields fell as the Fed hiked). At the zero lower bound, the rate loses room as a tool.
misconceptions: The central bank does not 'set all interest rates'; it targets one overnight rate and influences the rest of the curve only indirectly through expectations and operations.
example: In 2022–2023 the FOMC raised its target range for the federal funds rate from 0–0.25% to 5.25–5.50% in a series of moves of 25 to 75 basis points.

name: Overnight rate
definition: The interest rate on loans or deposits with a maturity of one business day, typically traded between financial institutions to manage daily reserve or cash positions. Key U.S. overnight rates include the effective federal funds rate (unsecured) and SOFR (secured by Treasury collateral).
intuition: It is the price of borrowing money until tomorrow — the shortest-maturity interest rate in the financial system and the anchor for all longer rates.
mechanics: Institutions lend and borrow cash for one day in money markets; transaction-level data are aggregated into published benchmarks (the New York Fed computes EFFR and SOFR as volume-weighted medians of overnight transactions). Central banks steer overnight rates to implement policy.
failure_modes: Overnight rates can spike under collateral or reserve scarcity (e.g. the September 2019 repo spike), breaking the link with the policy target; month- and quarter-end reporting effects also distort measured rates.
misconceptions: There is no single 'overnight rate': secured (repo/SOFR) and unsecured (fed funds) overnight rates coexist and can diverge because they price different risks and counterparties.
example: On a typical day, a bank lending reserves to another bank overnight earns the federal funds rate, while a money market fund lending cash against Treasury collateral earns a rate near SOFR.

citations.source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Effective Federal Funds Rate (EFFR)

name: Secured Overnight Financing Rate
definition: A broad measure of the cost of borrowing cash overnight collateralized by U.S. Treasury securities, published each business day by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. It is the principal U.S. dollar benchmark that replaced LIBOR for derivatives and loans.
intuition: It is the going rate for a one-day loan backed by Treasuries — essentially a near-risk-free overnight borrowing cost built from actual repo market transactions.
mechanics: SOFR is calculated as a volume-weighted median of transaction-level tri-party repo data, GCF Repo data, and bilateral Treasury repo cleared through FICC's DVP service (filtered to remove specials), and is published at approximately 8:00 a.m. ET each business day.
failure_modes: Because it is secured and transaction-based, SOFR can spike when repo funding is scarce (e.g. September 2019) and reflects collateral market conditions rather than bank credit risk; unlike LIBOR it has no term or credit component, complicating its use in loan pricing.
misconceptions: SOFR is not set by the Federal Reserve as a policy rate, nor is it a forecast — it is a backward-looking measure of realized overnight repo transactions.
example: A floating-rate note might pay 'SOFR + 80 bp', resetting its coupon off the daily-published SOFR benchmark.

name: Federal funds rate
definition: The interest rate at which depository institutions lend reserve balances to other depository institutions overnight, uncollateralized. The FOMC sets a target rate or range for it, and the New York Fed publishes the effective federal funds rate (EFFR) as the volume-weighted median of actual transactions.
intuition: It is the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of their reserve balances at the Fed — the rate U.S. monetary policy directly targets.
mechanics: The federal funds market consists of domestic unsecured overnight borrowings in U.S. dollars by depository institutions from other institutions, primarily GSEs. The EFFR is computed as a volume-weighted median of transactions reported on the FR 2420 report and published for the prior business day at about 9:00 a.m.; the Desk's operations keep it within the FOMC's target range.
failure_modes: The fed funds market is thin and dominated by specific players (GSEs lending to banks), so the EFFR can be unrepresentative of marginal funding costs; the rate also lost its role as the sole steering variable once abundant reserves made administered rates the main control tools.
misconceptions: The Fed does not directly set the market fed funds rate by decree — it sets a target range and uses operations and administered rates to steer the traded rate into it.
example: With an FOMC target range of 3.50–3.75%, the EFFR typically prints near the middle of the range, e.g. 3.62%.

name: Repo rate
definition: The implicit interest rate on a repurchase agreement, a transaction in which one party sells securities and agrees to repurchase them later at a slightly higher price — economically a loan collateralized by securities. The rate is set by the difference between the sale and repurchase prices relative to the term.
intuition: It is the cost of borrowing cash against bonds: you hand over the securities, get cash, and pay back a bit more later — that bit more, annualized, is the repo rate.
mechanics: In a repo the cash borrower sells securities and commits to repurchase them at a predetermined higher price; the price gap implies the repo interest. General collateral (GC) rates apply to non-specific securities, while repos on particular issues in high demand ('specials') trade at lower rates. The New York Fed uses repo and reverse repo operations to help keep the fed funds rate in its target range.
formula: Repo rate = ((repurchase price − sale price) / sale price) × (360 or 365 / term in days), per the market's day-count convention.
failure_modes: Repo rates can spike abruptly when collateral or dealer balance-sheet capacity is scarce (September 2019, March 2020), transmitting stress across funding markets; specialness can also drive individual-issue repo rates far below GC, distorting funding-cost readings.
misconceptions: A repo is not an outright sale of the bond for risk-transfer purposes — the seller retains the economic exposure and the obligation to repurchase, so it functions as secured borrowing.
example: A dealer sells $100 million of Treasuries overnight and agrees to repurchase them for $100.015 million; the implied overnight repo rate is about 5.4% annualized (0.015/100 × 360).

name: Haircut
definition: The percentage reduction applied to the market value of collateral when determining how much cash can be borrowed against it. In a repo, the haircut is the gap between the collateral's value and the cash lent, protecting the lender against a fall in collateral value before it could be sold.
intuition: If you pledge $1 million of bonds with a 5% haircut, the lender only gives you $950,000 — the haircut is the lender's safety cushion.
mechanics: Cash lent = collateral market value × (1 − haircut). Haircuts are set per asset class based on price volatility, liquidity, credit quality, and borrower risk; riskier or less liquid collateral receives larger haircuts.
formula: Loan amount = collateral value × (1 − h), where h is the haircut (e.g. h = 0.05 for 5%).
failure_modes: Haircuts set in calm times can prove inadequate in stressed markets when collateral gaps down in value; conversely, abrupt haircut increases force deleveraging and can propagate fire sales, as seen in 2008.
misconceptions: A haircut is not a fee or interest charge — it reduces the amount lent, not the price of the loan, and the full collateral value (less the loan) is returned when the repo unwinds.
example: Pledging $1,000,000 of Treasury bonds at a 2% haircut lets the borrower draw $980,000 in cash; the extra $20,000 of collateral covers the lender if bond prices fall.

citations.source: Investopedia, Haircut

name: Term premium
definition: The extra yield investors demand for holding a longer-term bond instead of rolling over a series of short-term instruments — compensation for the risk that future rates and inflation differ from expectations. It is the difference between a long-term yield and the expected average of future short rates, and it is not directly observable.
intuition: Locking your money up for ten years is riskier than renewing a one-year loan ten times; the term premium is the extra pay for bearing that risk.
mechanics: Estimated with term-structure models: a model (e.g. the Fed's Kim–Wright three-factor arbitrage-free model, published on FRED as THREEFYTP10) decomposes observed yields into expected short-rate paths plus a residual term premium. Estimates are model-dependent and can be negative.
formula: y(T) ≈ (1/T) × Σ E[short rate_t] + TP(T), where y(T) is the T-year yield and TP(T) the term premium.
failure_modes: Term premium estimates vary substantially across models and can flip sign with specification changes; using any single estimate as ground truth for 'rich/cheap' bonds is fragile.
misconceptions: The term premium is not a measured quantity like a yield — it is a model-implied residual, and a rising long yield does not tell you whether expectations or the premium moved without a model.
example: If the 10-year Treasury yields 4.5% while the expected average short rate over the decade is 4.0%, the model-implied 10-year term premium is about 0.5%.

citations.source: FRED, Term Premium on a 10 Year Zero Coupon Bond [THREEFYTP10] (source: Board of Governors, Kim and Wright 2005)

name: Breakeven inflation
definition: The inflation rate that would make an investor indifferent between holding a nominal Treasury and a same-maturity Treasury Inflation-Protected Security (TIPS), computed as the nominal yield minus the real (TIPS) yield. It is a market-based measure of expected average inflation over the horizon, though it also embeds inflation risk and liquidity premia.
intuition: If nominal bonds pay 4.5% and inflation-protected bonds pay 2.0%, the market is pricing roughly 2.5% average inflation — that gap is the breakeven.
mechanics: Computed from constant-maturity series, e.g. FRED's T10YIE = 10-Year Treasury Constant Maturity (DGS10) minus 10-Year Treasury Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity (DFII10); the latest value implies what market participants expect inflation to average over the next 10 years.
formula: Breakeven inflation ≈ y(nominal, T) − y(real TIPS, T); exactly, (1 + y_nom)/(1 + y_real) − 1 under compounding.
failure_modes: Breakevens mix inflation expectations with inflation risk premia and the liquidity disadvantage of TIPS, so they can diverge from true expectations — e.g. they collapsed in 2008 partly because TIPS became deeply illiquid, not because deflation was genuinely expected.
misconceptions: Breakeven inflation is not a pure forecast of CPI; it is the rate that equates two bond prices, so reading it as the market's literal inflation expectation ignores embedded premia.
example: With the 10-year nominal Treasury at 4.3% and the 10-year TIPS real yield at 2.0%, the 10-year breakeven inflation rate is about 2.3%.

citations.source: FRED, 10-Year Breakeven Inflation Rate [T10YIE] (source: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis)

name: Inflation swap
definition: A derivative in which one party pays a fixed rate and the other pays the realized change in an inflation index (e.g. U.S. CPI-U) on a notional amount, transferring inflation risk. In the standard zero-coupon form, both legs are compounded and exchanged as a single payment at maturity.
intuition: It is a bet or hedge on inflation itself: one side pays a pre-agreed inflation rate, the other pays whatever inflation actually turns out to be.
mechanics: The fixed leg compounds at the agreed fixed rate; the floating leg accrues the realized growth of the reference inflation index (USD uses CPI-U), typically with a publication lag of a few months. In a zero-coupon inflation swap the two compounded amounts are netted and paid once at maturity; the quoted fixed rate is the market's swap-implied inflation level.
formula: Fixed leg payment = N × [(1 + k)^n − 1]; inflation leg payment = N × [I(T)/I(0) − 1], where N is notional, k the fixed swap rate, n the tenor in years, and I the inflation index level.
failure_modes: Index publication lags, revisions, and seasonal patterns complicate pricing and hedging; the market is also less liquid than nominal swaps, and quoted rates embed inflation risk premia just like TIPS breakevens.
misconceptions: The fixed rate on an inflation swap is not a pure inflation forecast; like breakevens, it includes risk and liquidity premia, so it overstates or understates true expected inflation.
example: A pension fund enters a 10-year zero-coupon inflation swap paying a fixed 2.6% and receiving realized CPI-U growth on $50 million notional, hedging its inflation-linked liabilities.

citations.source: ICE (Intercontinental Exchange) SDX Interest Rates Help — Zero Coupon Inflation Swap
